Case Study 04 · Brand Personalization

Brand Manager: Letting Every Firm Own Its Brand

Designing a centralized brand management platform inside the Business Configurator — a single source of truth for logos and branding assets across advisors, institutions, and enterprise teams — so every firm controls how its identity shows up across every client touchpoint, without an engineering ticket for every logo or letterhead change.

Role

Domain

Scope

Methods
Current-State Audit, IA & Inheritance Modeling, Hi-Fi Prototyping
6 of 16

Separate, team-built logo tools replaced by a single governed logo repository in the Business Configurator

Overview

LPL Financial supports thousands of independent advisory firms and institutions, each with its own visual identity and its own expectations for how that identity should appear in client-facing materials. Before this work, every application or channel team — statements, letters, forms, reporting, account view — had built its own tool for managing logos, with no shared standard between them.

I led the design of Flexible Branding, which created a centralized brand management platform inside the Business Configurator — a single source of truth for logos and branding assets across advisors, institutions, and enterprise teams. Replacing fragmented, application-specific branding with a scalable, one-to-many distribution model gave LPL a future-ready capability: one that ensures brand consistency, simplifies governance, and accelerates delivery across current and future digital experiences.

Sixteen channels are expected to need branding in total; six are supported today — Statements, Letters, Forms: Print, Forms: Digital Notifications, Client Reporting, and Account View — with the remaining ten rolling in as the program expands.

The Problem

Because each channel team built its own logo-management tool independently, there was no shared standard for how a firm's brand should be stored or presented. That fragmentation showed up as inconsistency across nearly every dimension a logo touches:

  • Inconsistent file types and formats. One channel's tool expected TIFF, another JPEG, another PNG — with no shared convention for which format belonged where.
  • Inconsistent colors and resolutions. Color models (CMYK vs. RGB) and resolution requirements varied by tool, so the same logo could render correctly in one output and wrong in another.
  • Inconsistent file sizes and dimensions. Each tool enforced its own size and dimension limits, with no central reference for what a channel actually required.
  • Inconsistent file management locations. Logos lived wherever each team's tool happened to store them, so there was no single place to find, audit, or update a firm's current branding.

These inconsistencies weren't just an internal maintenance headache — they made customers upset. A firm might see its logo rendered crisply on a statement and blurry or off-brand on a client report, with no clear way to fix it themselves. The goal wasn't a branding "feature" bolted onto one more channel — it was a single, governed repository that every channel could draw from, so a firm's identity looked right everywhere, consistently.

Design Approach

I designed Flexible Branding as a single, centrally managed logo repository rather than a set of one-off branding tools scattered across each channel team. The core decision: logos are uploaded and governed once, per channel, in one place — and every downstream output reads from that same source instead of maintaining its own copy.

Upload once, per channel

Each of the 16 channels keeps its own technical requirements — format, dimensions, resolution, color model, file size — but every upload happens in the same governed repository instead of a separate team tool.

Organized by organization

Branding lives on the Business Configurator's org record, alongside Service Agreements, People, and Fee Settings — so brand management sits where every other firm-level configuration already lives.

Inherit down the hierarchy

A Parent Organization's branding applies to its DBA / Child Organizations by default, so a multi-entity firm doesn't have to re-upload the same logos for every sub-brand.

Override at the Rep ID level

When an individual rep needs a different logo than their firm's default — a co-branded practice, for example — "Assign logo by Rep ID" lets that be set as a granular exception, not a new ticket.

One governed logo repository drives all 16 branded channels — Account View, Statements, Letters, Forms, and Client Reporting shown here.

How It Works

The repository concept is easiest to see in the actual flow — from a firm's place in the org hierarchy down to a single advisor's override.

Every firm enters through its place in the org hierarchy. Pruman Financial Corp is a parent organization with four DBA offices — Smith Wealth Partners East, West, North, and South — visible right in the org switcher. Branding set at the parent cascades to all four by default.
The Branding tab is where all six channels converge, each with its own inherited spec (left). Uploading is a standard file picker — no special software, no engineering ticket (right).
Once uploaded, every channel shows its status at a glance (left). For the rare exception, an admin can override a single channel for a single Rep ID without disturbing the org-level default everyone else inherits (right).

Key Design Decisions

1. Treat the logo repository as infrastructure, not a per-channel field

The single most important framing decision was refusing to let each channel team keep its own logo tool. Instead of a logo field on the statements team's roadmap and a separate one on the client reporting team's roadmap, Flexible Branding lives in one repository and every channel is a consumer of that same source. That's what fixes the file type, format, color, resolution, size, and location inconsistencies at the root instead of patching each tool individually.

2. Respect each channel's real technical constraints

Centralizing the repository didn't mean forcing one spec onto every channel. A statement logo genuinely needs 300dpi CMYK TIFF art for print production; an Account View logo is a small PNG icon. I designed each upload card to surface its own format, dimension, resolution, and file-size requirements up front, so firms get it right the first time instead of trial-and-error rejections.

3. Model the org hierarchy, not just the firm

Firms aren't flat — a Parent Organization can have several DBA / Child Organizations (regional offices, sub-practices), and within those, individual reps identified by Rep ID. I designed branding to inherit down that hierarchy by default, with "Assign logo by Rep ID" as an explicit override path for the exceptions, rather than requiring every level to be configured independently.

Constraints I designed within

  • Six team-built tools, six sets of habits. Statements, Letters, Forms, Client Reporting, and Account View teams each had their own way of handling logos; the design had to be good enough that firms and internal ops would actually adopt one repository over six familiar ones.
  • Genuinely different technical specs per channel. Print-oriented channels (Statements, Letters) require production-grade TIFF/CMYK art at 300dpi; digital surfaces accept JPEG/PNG at web resolutions. The design had to hold both without pretending they're the same problem.
  • Multi-entity firm structures. Parent Organizations, DBA/Child Organizations, and individual Rep IDs each needed a coherent place in the branding model — including third-party downstream dependencies, like statement logos that get submitted to a print vendor (Broadridge) once approved.

Because the underlying requirements genuinely differ by channel — a printed statement logo needs 300dpi CMYK TIFF art; an Account View logo is a 40×44px PNG — the repository doesn't force one spec onto every channel. It centralizes where logos live and how they're managed, while keeping each channel's real technical constraints visible at the point of upload:

Status & Next Steps

In-flight program

Six of the sixteen expected channels are live: Statements, Letters, Forms: Print, Forms: Digital Notifications, Client Reporting, and Account View. Flexible Branding is rolling out as part of the broader Personalization program rather than shipping as a single release — the near-term focus is bringing the remaining ten channels onto the same repository and extending self-service configuration further out to firms directly.

Reflection

What made this project a design problem rather than a settings-page exercise was resisting the instinct to let each channel keep managing its own logo tool. The real work was recognizing that six independently built tools — each with its own file types, colors, resolutions, sizes, and storage locations — were all downstream of the same unmet need: a firm wanting to look like itself, consistently, everywhere. Designing one governed repository, with room for each channel's real constraints and a hierarchy that matches how firms are actually structured, is what turns "why doesn't my logo look right" from a support ticket into something a firm can just fix. It's also what makes the platform future-ready: a one-to-many distribution model means a seventeenth channel registers once and inherits the same governance, rather than repeating the fragmentation this project was built to undo.
